extracted.intended_audience: mathematics community and general readers interested in mathematical news and commentary (readers of the AMS blog)
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating claimed proofs of major problems
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for how members of the mathematical community and interested public should judge and react to high-profile claims of proofs for famous open problems (e.g., Riemann hypothesis). Emphasizes indicators of credibility, publication status, community scrutiny, and broader impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert scrutiny / convincing the community
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed proof should convince experts and withstand scrutiny from knowledgeable mathematicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: John Baez: “I bet that Atiyah’s claimed proof…will not convince experts.” The post emphasizes showing results to experts and obtaining their assessment; silence from experts or lack of convincing feedback is a warning sign. Historical examples cited where claimed proofs were shown to experts and failed to persuade (e.g., Atiyah’s earlier 12-page Feit–Thompson claim and 2016 arXiv paper).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and peer review status
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the underpinning work has been submitted to, accepted by, or published in reputable peer-reviewed venues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes Atiyah 'attributes much of the theoretical work ... to a paper of his own that has been submitted to the Proceedings of the Royal Society A' and that 'that paper has yet to be published.' Publication/peer review increases credibility; unpublished or not-yet-reviewed supporting papers are a reason for caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and level of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof should be sufficiently detailed and complete rather than overly short or sketchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Clay Institute’s 'Official Problem Description' for the Riemann hypothesis runs 11 pages, while 'Atiyah’s current write-up of the proof is five pages long.' Very brief write-ups for deep problems prompt skepticism; expect full arguments, explanations, and supporting work rather than terse claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: References and supporting literature
rubrics_metrics.description: A credible proof should be well-situated in the literature with an adequate bibliography and clear attribution to prior work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post observes that Atiyah’s list of references includes just three works (an unpublished paper, an Abel lecture, and Hirzebruch’s 1966 book). Sparse referencing or missing connections to foundational literature is a red flag; supporting and underpinning theoretical work should be cited and accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical soundness / absence of big holes
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments must be logically complete and free of significant gaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post cites a prior Atiyah arXiv paper whose 'argument was full of big holes.' Inspect proofs for logical gaps; large unproven steps or hand-wavy arguments indicate the claim is not yet a valid proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from proposer's prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: The validity of a proof does not depend on the proposer’s CV, awards, or reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commenter: 'The CV of a proposer of a mathematical proof is an irrelevant social factor with respect to the validity of the proof.' Evaluate the mathematical content on its own merits rather than the fame of the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track record of similar claims / historical skepticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful that many previous claimed proofs of famous problems have later been found invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes 'many other supposed proofs for the Riemann hypothesis have been proposed, only to fall apart under further scrutiny.' Historical frequency of false claims motivates cautious, evidence-based evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public announcement and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Making a claim public (lectures, blog posts, preprints) and sharing write-ups invites community evaluation and is part of the validation process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Atiyah presented a lecture at HLF and posted a five-page write-up; the post also references coverage in media and blogs. Public dissemination enables scrutiny and discussion, though it is not a substitute for peer-reviewed validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential positive value beyond correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a claimed proof is incorrect, it can be valuable by reigniting discussion and suggesting new directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author writes that Atiyah 'has already done something phenomenal: reignited a worldwide conversation about the Riemann hypothesis.' The social/scientific benefit of stimulating ideas and conversation is recognized as a separate metric from mathematical correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel or interdisciplinary approaches as promising but needing care
rubrics_metrics.description: Approaches that cross disciplinary boundaries (e.g., connections to physics) can be fruitful but require rigorous translation and validation within mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commenter notes Atiyah’s approach 'crosses over to physics' and that 'such approaches seem potentially fruitful.' Novel connections should be examined carefully for mathematical rigor and relevance to the problem.
